text: 1 Scope
trace: 1 Scope
text_preview: 1 Scope

text: The present document specifies the initial use cases that have been approved within O-RAN WG3. The purpose of the use cases is to help identify requirements for O-RAN defined interfaces and functions, specifically Near-RT RIC functions and E2 interface, eventually leading to formal drafting of interface specifications. For each use case, the document describes the motivation, resources, steps involved, and data requirements. Finally, the requirements clause details the functional and nonfunctional requirements derived from these use cases.

text: For the purposes of the present document, the terms and definitions \[given in 3GPP TR 21.905 \[i.1\] and the following\] apply. A term defined in the present document takes precedence over the definition of the same term, if any, in 3GPP TR 21.905 \[i.1\].
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: For the purposes of this document, terms and definitions from 3GPP TR 21.905 [i.1] apply. Definitions in this document take precedence over those in 3GPP TR 21.905 [i.1].

text: A1 policy: Type of declarative policies expressed using formal statements that enable the Non-RT RIC function in the SMO to guide the Near-RT RIC function, and hence the RAN, towards better fulfilment of the RAN intent.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: A1 policy: Type of declarative policies expressed using formal statements that enable the Non-RT RIC function in the SMO to guide the Near-RT RIC function, and hence the RAN, towards better fulfilment of the RAN intent.

text: A1 enrichment information: Information utilized by Near-RT RIC that is collected or derived at SMO/Non-RT RIC either from non-network data sources or from network functions themselves.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: A1 enrichment information: Information utilized by Near-RT RIC that is collected or derived at SMO/Non-RT RIC either from non-network data sources or from network functions themselves.

text: A1-policy based traffic steering process mode: An operational mode in which the Near-RT RIC is configured through A1 policy to use traffic steering actions to ensure a more specific notion of network performance \(for example, applying to smaller groups of E2 nodes and UEs in the RAN\) than that which it ensures in the background traffic steering.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: A1-policy based traffic steering process mode: An operational mode where the Near-RT RIC is configured through A1 policy to use traffic steering actions, focusing on smaller groups of E2 nodes and UEs for more specific network performance.

text: Background traffic steering processing mode: An operational mode in which the Near-RT RIC is configured through O1 to use traffic steering actions to ensure a general background network performance which applies broadly across E2 nodes and UEs in the RAN.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: Background traffic steering processing mode: An operational mode in which the Near-RT RIC is configured through O1 to use traffic steering actions to ensure a general background network performance which applies broadly across E2 nodes and UEs in the RAN.

text: Baseline RAN behavior: The default RAN behavior as configured at the E2 nodes by SMO.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: Baseline RAN behavior: The default RAN behavior as configured at the E2 nodes by SMO.

text: E2: Interface connecting the Near-RT RIC and one or more O-CU-CPs, one or more O-CU-UPs, one or more O-DUs, and one or more O-eNBs.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: E2: Interface connecting the Near-RT RIC and one or more O-CU-CPs, one or more O-CU-UPs, one or more O-DUs, and one or more O-eNBs.

text: E2 node: A logical node terminating E2 interface. In the present document, O-RAN nodes terminating E2 interface are:
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: E2 node: A logical node terminating E2 interface. In the present document, O-RAN nodes terminating E2 interface are:

text:
* for NR access: O-CU-CP, O-CU-UP, O-DU or any combination.
  * for E-UTRA access: O-eNB.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview:
* for NR access: O-CU-CP, O-CU-UP, O-DU or any combination.
  * for E-UTRA access: O-eNB.

text: FCAPS: Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, Security.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: FCAPS: Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, Security.

text: Intents: A declarative policy to steer or guide the behavior of RAN functions, allowing the RAN function to calculate the optimal result to achieve stated objective.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: Intents: A declarative policy to steer or guide the behavior of RAN functions, allowing the RAN function to calculate the optimal result to achieve stated objective.

text: Non-RT RIC \(O-RAN Non-Real-Time RAN Intelligent Controller\): A logical function that enables non-real-time control and optimization of RAN elements and resources, AI/ML workflow including model training and updates, and policy-based guidance of applications/features in Near-RT RIC.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: Non-RT RIC \(O-RAN Non-Real-Time RAN Intelligent Controller\): A logical function that enables non-real-time control and optimization of RAN elements and resources, AI/ML workflow including model training and updates, and policy-based guidance of applications/features in Near-RT RIC.

text: Near-RT RIC \(O-RAN Near-Real-Time RAN Intelligent Controller\): A logical function that enables near-real-time control and optimization of RAN elements and resources via fine-grained \(e.g., UE basis, cell basis\) data collection and actions over E2 interface.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: Near-RT RIC \(O-RAN Near-Real-Time RAN Intelligent Controller\): A logical function that enables near-real-time control and optimization of RAN elements and resources via fine-grained \(e.g., UE basis, cell basis\) data collection and actions over E2 interface.

text: O-CU \(O-RAN Central Unit\): A logical node hosting RRC, SDAP and PDCP protocols.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: O-CU \(O-RAN Central Unit\): A logical node hosting RRC, SDAP and PDCP protocols.

text: O-CU-CP \(O-RAN Central Unit – Control Plane\): A logical node hosting the RRC and the control plane part of the PDCP protocol.

text_preview: O-CU-CP \(O-RAN Central Unit – Control Plane\): A logical node hosting the RRC and the control plane part of the PDCP protocol.

text: O-CU-UP \(O-RAN Central Unit – User Plane\): A logical node hosting the user plane part of the PDCP protocol and the SDAP protocol.

text: O-DU \(O-RAN Distributed Unit\): A logical node hosting RLC/MAC/High-PHY layers based on a lower layer functional split.

text: O-RU \(O-RAN Radio Unit\): A logical node hosting Low-PHY layer and RF processing based on a lower layer functional split. This is similar to 3GPP's "TRP" or "RRH" but more specific in including the Low-PHY layer \(FFT/iFFT, PRACH extraction\).

text_preview: O-RU (O-RAN Radio Unit): A logical node hosting Low-PHY layer and RF processing based on a lower layer functional split, similar to 3GPP's "TRP" or "RRH", but with added specificity including FFT/iFFT and PRACH extraction.

text: RAN UE group: Aggregations of UEs whose grouping is set in the E2 nodes through E2 procedures also based on the scope of A1 policies. These groups can then be the target of E2 CONTROL or POLICY messages.

text_preview: RAN UE group: Aggregations of UEs whose grouping is set in the E2 nodes through E2 procedures also based on the scope of A1 policies. These groups can then be the target of E2 CONTROL or POLICY messages.

text: Traffic steering action: The use of a mechanism to alter RAN behavior. Such actions include E2 procedures such as CONTROL and POLICY.
trace: 3.1 Terms
text_preview: Traffic steering action: The use of a mechanism to alter RAN behavior. Such actions include E2 procedures such as CONTROL and POLICY.

text: Traffic steering inner loop: The part of the traffic steering processing, triggered by the arrival of periodic TS related KPM \(Key Performance Measurement\) from E2 node, which includes UE grouping, setting additional data collection from the RAN, as well as selection and execution of one or more optimization actions to enforce traffic steering policies.
trace: 3.1 Terms

text: Traffic steering outer loop: The part of the traffic steering processing, triggered by the Near-RT RIC setting up or updating traffic steering aware resource optimization procedure based on information from A1 policy setup or update, A1 Enrichment Information \(EI\) and/or outcome of Near-RT RIC evaluation, which includes the initial configuration \(preconditions\) and injection of related A1 policies, triggering conditions for TS changes.

text_preview: Traffic steering outer loop: Triggered by Near-RT RIC setup or update, based on A1 policy info, EI, and RIC evaluation outcomes. Includes preconditions and injected A1 policies, triggering TS changes.

text: Traffic steering processing mode: An operational mode in which either the RAN or the Near-RT RIC is configured to ensure a particular network performance. This performance includes such aspects as cell load and throughput, and it can apply differently to different E2 nodes and UEs. Throughout this process, traffic steering actions are used to fulfill the requirements of this configuration.

text: 4.1.1 Background and goal of the use case
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: 4.1.1 Background and goal of the use case

text: The rapid traffic growth and multiple frequency bands utilized in a commercial network make it challenging to steer the traffic in a balanced distribution. Typical controls are limited to adjusting the cell reselection and handover parameters; and modifying load calculations and cell priorities.
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: The rapid traffic growth and multiple frequency bands utilized in a commercial network make it challenging to steer the traffic in a balanced distribution. Typical controls are limited to adjusting the cell reselection and handover parameters; and modifying load calculations and cell priorities.

text: The goal of Near-RT RIC traffic steering is to interpret the policies received over A1 and to determine the optimum changes it can make towards achieving those goals. It may also leverage the A1 enrichment information. Traffic steering may reuse mechanisms provided by other use cases to effect the changes necessary to achieve its goals.
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: The goal of Near-RT RIC traffic steering is to interpret the policies received over A1 and to determine the optimum changes it can make towards achieving those goals. It may also leverage the A1 enrichment information. Traffic steering may reuse mechanisms provided by other use cases to effect the changes necessary to achieve its goals.

text: More specifically, Near-RT RIC triggers E2 procedure and related control/policies so as to obtain network performance that would fulfill the criteria identified in the A1 policies.

* 1\) OAM functions in SMO domain: 
    * Collect necessary measurement metrics from network level measurement report and enrichment data \(can acquire data from application\) for constructing/training relevant AI/ML models.

  * 2\) Non-RT RIC in SMO domain: 
    * Send A1 policies and receive policy feedback to/from Near-RT RIC to drive resource optimization at RAN level.
    * E.g., TS targets as specified in O-RAN.WG2.A1AP \[24\].

text: In this clause the possible processing modes of traffic steering are described. Three general traffic steering processing modes and the transitions between them are shown in figure 4.1.3-1.
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.3 Solutions
text_preview: In this clause the possible processing modes of traffic steering are described. Three general traffic steering processing modes and the transitions between them are shown in figure 4.1.3-1.

text: These modes represent the way the Near-RT RIC \(or RAN\) operates on a given group of UEs, and not the operation of any component as a whole. As such, the Near-RT RIC, could be operating in both modes 1 and 2 concurrently for different sets of UEs. For example, the transition from mode 0 or 1 to 2 occurs only for a group of UE defined by the A1 policy scope. At the same time, other UE groups may still be handled in mode 0 and/or 1.
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.3 Solutions
text_preview: The Near-RT RIC operates on multiple UEs in modes 1 and 2, not as a whole component. It can run both modes concurrently for different sets of UEs. Transition from mode 0/1 to 2 occurs within specific UE groups defined by A1 policy scope, while others remain in modes 0 and/or 1.

text: The three processing modes are described in more detail below:
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.3 Solutions
text_preview: The three processing modes are described in more detail below:

text:
* 0\. "Baseline" traffic steering behavior: OAM functions in SMO domain uses O1 configuration on one or more E2 node to set up a desired baseline behavior. This also sets up baseline performance monitoring of E2 node by the SMO. In this mode, Near-RT RIC is not involved.
  * 1\. "Background" Near-RT RIC processing: OAM functions in SMO domain uses O1 configuration of Near-RT RIC to set up a desired "background Near-RT RIC behavior". In this mode the Near-RT RIC sets up E2 mechanisms to monitor E2 node and uses traffic steering related E2 mechanisms to achieve the desired background behavior of the set of E2 nodes connected to the Near-RT RIC.
  * 2\. "A1-policy based" Near-RT RIC processing: This mode can be entered from either mode 0 or mode 1. Non-RT RIC in SMO domain uses A1-P to specify an A1 guided behavior for a targeted subset of E2 nodes or UEs. If entering this from mode 1, this will have the effect of modifying the existing Near-RT RIC "background" behavior to include a more specific A1 guided behavior. In this mode, the Near-RT RIC can either set up or modify E2 mechanisms used to monitor

text: Processing mode 2 contain an 'outer loop' and an 'inner loop'. In the inner loop, a number of different "E2 mechanism" can be used \(policy, report/control or insert/control\) towards a number of different target RAN functions in order to either exercise existing RAN mechanisms or modifying their ongoing behavior. The appropriate mechanism and target RAN function would depend upon the RAN function capabilities to support a given E2 mechanism, the A1-P scope and policy, the O1 configuration of the RIC and the performance observed through E2 monitoring.

text: Mobility control: Serving cell can be chosen based on the resource status and QoS of the UE\(s\) targeted by an A1 traffic steering policy. Moreover, load balancing can be achieved to improve the overall network performance. The following procedures can be used for traffic steering:
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.4 Required data --> 4.1.4.1 Control over E2
text_preview: Mobility control: Serving cell can be chosen based on the resource status and QoS of the UE\(s\) targeted by an A1 traffic steering policy. Moreover, load balancing can be achieved to improve the overall network performance. The following procedures can be used for traffic steering:

text:
* Handover from the source cell to the target cell  
  * Configuration/reconfiguration of handover restriction list
  * Configuration of idle mode mobility parameters
  * Enable, disable, or modify CA \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.300 \[14\], 3GPP TS 36.300 \[8\], 3GPP TS 38.473 \[21\], 3GPP TS 38.331 \[18\] and 3GPP TS 36.331 \[11\]\)
  * Enable, disable, or modify dual connectivity \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.300 \[14\], 3GPP TS 36.300 \[8\], 3GPP TS 37.340 \[13\], 3GPP TS 38.473 \[21\], 3GPP TS 38.331 \[18\] and 3GPP TS 36.331 \[11\]\)
trace: 4.1 Traffic steering --> 4.1.4 Required data --> 4.1.4.1 Control over E2
text_preview:
Handover from source to target cell:

* Configure handover restriction list
* Set idle mode mobility parameters
* Modify CA settings (3GPP TS 38.300)
* Enable/disable/dual connect settings (3GPP TS 38.300)

text: Both RIC POLICY and RIC CONTROL can be used.

text: 4.2.1 Background and goal of the use case
trace: 4.2 QoS based resource optimization --> 4.2.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: 4.2.1 Background and goal of the use case

text: The network shall offer means to prioritize resources while preserving the required QoS properties, e.g., reliability, latency, bandwidth requirements, as specified in 3GPP TS 23.203 \[2\]. Current RAN network coverage and capacity depends on rigorous planning and configuration. However, due to varying nature of traffic demands and radio channels as well as multiple services to co-exist, it is hard to satisfy all QoS requirements simultaneously.
trace: 4.2 QoS based resource optimization --> 4.2.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: The network shall prioritize resources while preserving required QoS properties (reliability, latency, bandwidth) as specified in 3GPP TS 23.203. Current RAN coverage and capacity depend on rigorous planning and configuration, but satisfying all QoS requirements simultaneously is challenging due to varying traffic demands and radio channels.

text: In summary, it is important for an E2 node to achieve QoS targets as smoothly as possible. The QoS aware resource optimization should provide a refined granularity of radio resource allocation based on varying radio conditions and traffics in order to meet the diverse requirements of reliability, latency, and bandwidth simultaneously. In addition, it should coordinate allocation of radio resources for co-existing multiple services, which may have different priorities, to achieve the optimal utilization of radio resources.
trace: 4.2 QoS based resource optimization --> 4.2.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: Achieving QoS targets smoothly is crucial for E2 nodes. A QoS-aware resource optimization should provide refined granularity in radio resource allocation based on varying conditions and traffic, meeting diverse requirements for reliability, latency, and bandwidth. It should also coordinate resource allocation for co-existing services with different priorities to optimize utilization.

text: In case when the network performance data is observed outside the boundary of the defined QoS targets, the Near-RT RIC should be able to trigger re-allocation of radio resources so that the QoS indicators can move back within limits outlined in the A1 policies.

@startuml
    skinparam ParticipantPadding 4
    skinparam BoxPadding 8
    skinparam defaultFontSize 12
    Box "Service Management and Orchestration" #gold
     Participant OF as "OAM Functions"
     Participant non as "Non-RT RIC"
    End box
    Box "O-RAN" #lightpink
     Participant near as "Near-RT RIC" 
     Participant ran as "E2 Node" 
    End box
    group OUTER LOOP CONTROL
    ran <-> OF : <<O1>> RAN data collection
    OF -> non : Collected data
    non -> non : Collected data evaluation & QoS target generation
    non -> near : <<A1-P>> A1 policy setup or update
    near -> near : QoS optimization initiated
    group INNER LOOP CONTROL
     near -> ran : <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST (UE context and/or Measurement metrics)
     ran -> near : <<E2>> RIC INDICATION (UE context and/or Measurement metrics)
          non -> near : (opt.) <<A1-EI>> QoS related A1 Enrichment Information
     near -> near : QoS performance monitoring
     near -> ran : (opt.) <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST (QoS optimization RIC POLICY)
     near -> ran : (opt.) <<E2>> RIC CONTROL REQUEST (QoS optimization RIC CONTROL)
    end
    OF <- near : (opt.) <<O1>> QoS optimization related performance information
    OF -> non : (opt.) Performance information
    non -> non : QoS optimization performance evaluation
    end
    non -> near : <<A1-P>> A1 policy delete
    near -> ran : <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION DELETE
    @enduml

text:
* 1\) DRB control: RB control can be applied for modification of the following QoS properties:   
    * DRB QoS modification \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.473 \[21\] and 3GPP TS 23.501 \[3\]\): The DRB level QoS may be tuned to accommodate A1 policy requirement.
    * QoS flow remapping \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.473 \[21\]\): The mapping relationship between QoS flows and DRBs may be adjusted.
    * Logical channel reconfiguration \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.331 \[18\] and 3GPP TS 36.331 \[11\]\): The relevant parameters can be considered, e.g., priority, prioritized bit rate, bucket size duration, etc.
    * Radio admission control \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.331 \[18\] and 3GPP TS 36.331 \[11\]\): DRB admission control such as reject, or release may be applied.
    * Modification of dual-connectivity DRB \(as specified in 3GPP TS 37.340 \[13\]\): Change of bearer termination point \(MN or SN\) and/or bearer types \(MCG/SCG/split\), and control of split ratio for a split bearer.
    * Activation and deactivation of packet duplication and configuration of the number of legs in DC, CA, or DC+CA scenarios \(as specified in 3GPP TS 36.300 \[8\] and 3GPP TS 38.300 \[14\]\).

    * SR periodicity reconfiguration \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.331 \[18\] and 3GPP TS 36.331 \[11\]\): Both sr-ProhibitTimer and sr-TransMax can be treated.
    * SPS configuration \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.331 \[18\] and 3GPP TS 36.331 \[11\]\): Both SPS-Config \(DL\) and ConfiguredGrantConfig \(UL\) can be treated.
    * Reconfiguration of slice level PRB quota \(as specified in 3GPP TS 28.541 \[4\]\)
    * Configuration of CQI table with certain target block error rate \(as specified in 3GPP TS 38.214 \[15\]\)

text:
* 3\) Radio access control: Depending on operator's policies, deployment scenarios, subscriber profiles, and available services, different criterion will be used in determining which access attempt should be allowed or blocked when congestion occurs in the system, as specified in 3GPP TS 22.261 \[1\]. For example, access control may be applied to restrict access of other UEs for a specific cell in order to achieve better QoS for some UEs. A cell-level, UE-level, or slice-level access control can be applied. Four categories of radio access control are indicated as below:

    * RRC connection reject
    * RRC connection release
    * Access barring

text: 4.3 RAN slice SLA assurance
trace: 4.3 RAN slice SLA assurance
text_preview: 4.3 RAN slice SLA assurance

text: The 3GPP standards architected a sliceable 5G infrastructure which allows creation and management of customized networks to meet specific service requirements that can be demanded by future applications, services and business verticals. Such a flexible architecture needs different requirements to be specified in terms of functionality, performance and group of users which can greatly vary from one service to the other. The 5G standardization efforts have gone into defining specific slices and their Service Level Agreements \(SLAs\) based on application/service type as specified in 3GPP TS 22.261 \[1\]. Since network slicing is conceived to be an end-to-end feature that includes the core network, the transport network and the radio access network \(RAN\), these requirements should be met at any slice subnet during the life-time of a network slice as specified in 3GPP TS 28.530 \[4\], especially in RAN side. Exemplary slice performance requirements are specified in terms of throughput, energy efficiency, latency and reliability at a high level in SDOs such as 3GPP TS 22.261 \[1\] and GSMA \[22\]. These requirements are defined as a reference for SLA/contractual agreements for each slice, which individually need proper handling in NG-RAN.
trace: 4.3 RAN slice SLA assurance
text_preview: the 3 gpp standards created a flexible 5 g infrastructure allowing customized networks with specific service requirements . this architecture requires different specifications for functionality , performance , and user groups . network slicing includes core , transport , and ran components , requiring specifications to be met at any slice subnet during its lifetime . key performance requirements include throughput , energy efficiency

text: Although network slicing support is started to be defined with 3GPP Release 15, slice assurance mechanisms in RAN needs to be further addressed to achieve deployable network slicing in an open RAN environment. It is necessary to assure the SLAs by dynamically controlling slice configurations based on slice specific performance information. Existing RAN performance measurements as specified in 3GPP TS 28.552 \[6\] and information model definitions as specified in 3GPP TS 28.541 \[5\] are not enough to support RAN slice SLA assurance use cases. This use case is intended to clarify necessary mechanisms and parameters for RAN slice SLA assurance.
trace: 4.3 RAN slice SLA assurance
text_preview: Network slicing support with 3GPP Release 15 has started, but RAN slice assurance mechanisms need further development for open RAN environments. To assure SLAs, dynamic control of slice configurations based on performance information is necessary. Existing RAN measurements are insufficient to support RAN slice SLA assurance use cases.

text: In the context of the RAN, the SLA assurance parameters sent over the A1 interface help the Near-RT RIC guide the behavior of the E2 nodes \(O-CU-UP, O-CU-CP, O-DU\). The Non-RT RIC utilizes the slice SLA information and performance metrics to derive the necessary set of A1 policies and sends those to the Near-RT RICs related to a network slice. Each subtending Near-RT RICs uses these A1 policies for further cell-level and/or UE-level policy guidance and/or control action over the E2 interface that affects the cells and/or UEs, involved in the network slice, served by the respective E2 nodes. The combined guidance is handled as one or more A1 policies and/or E2 policies and/or E2 control actions. The intention of the SLA assurance parameters in the RAN context is to provide guidance to the E2 nodes for assuring SLAs of the network slices in the radio access network.

text: 5G core and O-RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement
trace: 4.3.1 Background and goal of the use case --> 5G core and O-RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement
text_preview: 5G core and O-RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement

description: The diagram illustrates the architecture and interactions between 5G Core Network components and 5G RAN Network elements.
text: Figure 4.3.1-1: Core & RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement
trace: 4.3.1 Background and goal of the use case --> 5G core and O-RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement --> Figure 4.3.1-1: Core & RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement
text_preview: Figure 4.3.1-1: Core & RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement

text: The network functions and components that are related with SLA enforcement within 5G Core \(5GC\) and O-RAN are shown in figure 4.3.1-1. Although the 5GC enforces most of the SLA parameters, the components of the 5GC have a comprehensive view of the entire wireless network but from a core perspective. 3GPP Release 17 introduces the concept of a Network Slice Admission  Control Function \(NSACF\). This debuted from the 3GPP TR 23.700-40 \[i.3\], and normative as specified in 3GPP TS 23.501 \[31\], clause 5.15.11. The purpose of the NSACF is to enforce some of the slice SLA parameters from a 5G core perspective. While NSACF handles slice-specific user admission control into the network as specified in GSMA NG.116 \[22\] GST criterion, the AMF allows the UE to access slice\(s\) through S-NSSAI or NSSAI requests through NSACF interaction. Together, they can perform network-level policy enforcement. However, these components do not have the detailed knowledge of RAN, such as RAN resources usage or where specific UEs are geographically located within a gNB. These 5GC components can perform only at a "network view" and they also do not have control over RAN resources.
trace: 4.3.1 Background and goal of the use case --> 5G core and O-RAN cooperation for SLA enforcement
text_preview: The 5GC enforces most SLA parameters from a core perspective. The Network Slice Admission Control Function (NSACF) in 3GPP Release 17 handles slice-specific user admission control, interacts with AMF for UE access, and performs network-level policy enforcement, but lacks RAN resource knowledge and UEs' geographic locations.

description:
The diagram shows interactions concerning a 55G RAN Network:

1. "Non-RT RIC Information Exchange" from Non-RT RIC to E2 Nodes
2. "RAN Guidance Communication" from Near-RT RICs to E2 Nodes
3. "A1 Policy Decomposition" from near-RT RICs to E2 Nodes
4. "E2 Nodes Feedback" from E2 Nodes to Near-RT RICs
5. "SLA Assurance Policy Enforcement" from Near-RT RIC to E2 Nodes
6. "RAN Level Guidance to 55GC" from E2 Nodes to RAN & 5GC 

The diagram highlights the flow of RAN guidance, SLA assurance policy enforcement, and communication between different entities such as Non-RT RIC, near-RT RICs, E2 Nodes, and RAN & 5GC within a 55G RAN network.
text: Figure 4.3.1-2: Non-RT RIC & Near-RT RIC RAN guidance
trace: 4.3.1 Background and goal of the use case --> Non-RT RIC & Near-RT RIC provide RAN guidance for SLA objectives --> Figure 4.3.1-2: Non-RT RIC & Near-RT RIC RAN guidance
text_preview: Figure 4.3.1-2: Non-RT RIC & Near-RT RIC RAN guidance

text: As shown in figure 4.3.1-2, the Non-Real Time RIC obtains the SLA parameters from SMO. The Non-RT RIC has a system level view of RAN topology, configuration and performance, so rApps can provide ongoing guidance and decompose SLA objects to the subtending Near-RT RICs. The Non-RT RIC then translates the SLA parameters into SLA objective A1 policies to its subtending Near-RT RIC\(s\). In some cases, the SLA parameters are already RAN or UE specific. Those SLA parameters would then not need any change in their values and would be "passed-through" to the Near-RT RIC\(s\) in A1 policies.
trace: 4.3.1 Background and goal of the use case --> Non-RT RIC & Near-RT RIC provide RAN guidance for SLA objectives
text_preview: The Non-Real Time RIC obtains SLA parameters from SMO. With a system-level view of RAN topology, rApps provide ongoing guidance and decompose SLA objects for subtending Near-RT RICs. The Non-RT RIC translates SLA parameters into A1 policies for its subtending Near-RT RICs.

text: The Near-RT RICs obtain the SLA objectives via A1 policies from the Non-RT RIC. The Near-RT RIC can provide cell-level and/or UE-level guidance or control to the E2 nodes to achieve SLA assurance enforcement at the RAN level. The E2 nodes receive guidance or control from their respective Near-RT RICs. There are parameters as specified in GSMA GST/NEST NG.116 \[22\], such as the Downlink and Uplink Throughput Per Network Slice, that have both core and RAN applicability.
trace: 4.3.1 Background and goal of the use case --> Non-RT RIC & Near-RT RIC provide RAN guidance for SLA objectives
text_preview: Near-RT RICs obtain SLA objectives via A1 policies from Non-RT RIC. They provide cell-level guidance for SLA assurance at RAN level, receiving parameters like Downlink/Upstream Throughput Per Network Slice.

text: For example, the Downlink and Uplink Throughput Per Network Slice can be used by 5GC network functions; and the Non-RT RIC can calculate maxUlThptPerSlice and maxDlThptPerSlice parameters in an A1 policy which will then be used by the Near-RT RIC as target values via monitoring E2 node performance and, where required, requesting appropriate E2 services \(CONTROL and/or POLICY\) to provide guidance to the E2 nodes.

@startuml
    skinparam ParticipantPadding 4

    Box "Service Management and Orchestration" #gold

    group OUTER LOOP CONTROL

    OF -> non : RAN Slice SLA assurance data
    non -> non : Collected data evaluation and policy creation
    non -> near : <<A1>> SLA Assurance policy setup or update
    group INNER LOOP CONTROL
     near -> ran : <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST (REPORT, UE context & Measurement 
    metrics)

     near -> near : Evaluation, possible SLA violation prevention
     near -> ran : (opt.) <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST (POLICY)
    near -> ran : (opt.) <<E2>> RIC CONTROL REQUEST (Slice SLA assurance RIC CONTROL)
    end
    non <-- near: (opt.) <<A1>> A1 Policy feedback
    end

text: The E2 measurements are necessary for inference and prediction in the Near-RT RIC as the driver for decisions in addition to KPMs. For the slice SLA assurance use case, the Near-RT RIC can translate an A1 policy \(relatively static targets\) into a flexible selection of controls over E2 \(e.g., PRB control, access control\) by taking into account the runtime status in the Near-RT RIC. Therefore, it is required to specify those measurement parameters as possible as needed over E2 interface.

autonumber
    Box "Service Management and Orchestration" #gold
     Participant "Collection & Control" as smo
     Participant "Non-RT RIC" as non
    End box
    Box "O-RAN" #lightpink
     Participant near as "Near-RT RIC"
     Participant ran as "O-DU" 
    End box
    Box "External" #lightcyan
     Participant "Application Server" as app
    End box
    group Data Collection
     smo -> ran : <<O1>> Request the number of supported Non-GoB BF modes
     ran -> smo : <<O1>> Collect the number of supported Non-GoB BF modes
     smo -> non : Retrieve collected information
     smo -> ran : <<O1>> Request measurement data and RAN configurations for each Non-GoB BF mode
     ran -> smo : <<O1>> Collect measurement data and RAN configurations for each Non-GoB BF mode
     app -> smo : Collect enrichment information (e.g., UE location/mobility, etc.)
     smo -> non : Retrieve collected data
    end
    group AI/ML workflow
     non -> non : Associate enrichment information with \n measurements and configurations
     non -> non : Train AI/ML models to select \n the best Non-GoB mode
     non -> near: <<O1>> or <<O2>> \n Deploy AI/ML models
    end
    group Performance evaluation and optimization
     smo -> ran : <<O1>> Request measurement data and RAN configurations for each Non-GoB BF mode 
     ran -> smo : <<O1>> Collect measurement data and RAN configurations for each Non-GoB BF mode 
     app -> smo : Collect enrichment information (e.g., UE location/mobility, etc.)
     smo -> non : Retrieve collected data
     non -> non : Performance monitoring & evaluation
     non -> non : Re-train AI/ML models
     non -> near: <<O1>> or <<O2>> \n Update AI/ML models
    end
    @enduml

trace: 4.4 Massive MIMO optimization --> 4.4.2 Entities/resources involved in the use case --> 4.4.3 Solutions --> 4.4.3.2 Beam-based Mobility Robustness Optimization \(bMRO\)
text_preview: 4.4.3.2 Beam-based Mobility Robustness Optimization \(bMRO\)

text: Beam-based Mobility Robustness Optimization \(bMRO\) is an autonomous self-optimizing algorithm that improves beam-based inter-cell mobility performance by applying beam-specific HO parameters including Cell Individual Offsets \(CIO\), Time to Trigger \(TTT\), T310 counter, etc. on the handover configuration between neighbor cells, based on the analysis of beam-specific mobility-related counters and/or mobility failure events. bMRO is capable to reduce the number of unnecessary handovers, handover failures as well as ping-pong handovers particularly in cells that cover areas with different mobility characteristics.

text_preview: Beam-Based Mobility Robustness Optimization (bMRO) is an autonomous self-optimizing algorithm that improves beam-based inter-cell mobility by applying HO parameters to neighbor cell handover configurations, reducing unnecessary handovers and failures in areas with varying mobility characteristics.

text: Performance, complexity and gain analysis has been provided in O-RAN.WG1.mMIMO-Use-Cases-TR-v01.00 \[i.2\], clause 3.3. Signaling overhead and complexity \(RRC re-configuration, mobility reporting and O-CU reconfiguration messages\) can be further reduced by beam grouping in which case beams with similar mobility characteristics comprise a beam group \(e.g., group 1: low mobility pedestrian area, group 2: high mobility street\). Mobility reports consist of aggregated mobility KPI/PMs \(e.g., number of too early HOs, number of too late HOs, number of HO to wrong cell\) or individual failure reports with root cause \(e.g., to early HO, too late HO, HO to wrong cell\) or a combination of the two. Reports are sent per each SSB beam or SSB beam group towards each neighbor cell. Individual mobility failure reports will also be reported per UE to allow UE or UE groupbased optimization \(besides beam or beam group specific reporting\). While aggregated mobility KPIs/PMs are used for slow adaptations \(e.g., 5 min\), individual failure reports are used for faster adaptations \(e.g., 100 ms\) or for AI/ML based analysis of failure patterns. Measurement reporting periodicity and measurement type are configurable on a per cell basis considering the tradeoff between gain in mobility performance and associated signaling overhead. Mobility KPIs and failure events are forwarded from the O-CU to the Near-RT RIC, and the Near-RT RIC configures the CIO and the measurement reporting in the O-CUs. CIOs might be beam- or beam group-based and can also be configurable per UE group \(e.g., UE type, UE mobility or UE mode such as energy saving mode\).
trace: 4.4 Massive MIMO optimization --> 4.4.2 Entities/resources involved in the use case --> 4.4.3 Solutions --> 4.4.3.2 Beam-based Mobility Robustness Optimization \(bMRO\)
text_preview: Beam grouping reduces signaling overhead by aggregating KPIs/PMs or individual failure reports based on mobility characteristics. Reports are sent via SSB beam or group, enabling UE-based optimization and slow adaptations for AI analysis. Measurement reporting is configurable per-cell, balancing performance gain and signaling overhead.

text: While AI/ML based approaches are not mandated, AI/ML methods/models can be used i\) to build beam groups, to ii\) decide on cell individual measurement configuration, to iii\) detect changes in mobility characteristics \(e.g., traffic jam\) that trigger optimization, to iv\) group UEs in UE groups as well as v\) for the bMRO optimization algorithm itself to calculate the optimal cell individual offsets. In case of dynamic beam pattern optimization, relevant mMIMO beam pattern information shall be available at the Near-RT RIC, e.g., mobility reports might indicate a specific beam pattern.

In dynamic beam pattern optimization, relevant mMIMO beam pattern info is available at Near-RT RIC.

text: weights \(for transmission in the downlink\). This is unlike the non-GoB-based massive MIMO transmission used primarily in TDD systems, which do not involve CSI-based beamforming, but which involve periodic Sounding Reference Signals \(SRS\) transmission in the uplink by the UE to the O-DU for determining the appropriate UE-specific beamforming weights based on channel reciprocity. Hence, GoB-based massive MIMO transmissions incur a higher overhead due to periodic transmission of CSI-feedback from the UE towards enabling the selection of optimal beamforming weights for the UE.
trace: 4.4 Massive MIMO optimization --> 4.4.2 Entities/resources involved in the use case --> 4.4.3.4 AI/ML based CSI-RS and DMRS configuration optimization
text_preview: Weights for downlink transmission differ in TDD systems using Sounding Reference Signals (SRS) uplink, which determine UE-specific beamforming weights based on channel reciprocity. GoB-based transmissions incur higher overhead due to periodic CSI-feedback transmission from the UE to enable optimal weight selection.

text: Furthermore, based on the relevant configuration by O-CU-CP, the O-DU transmits the Demodulation Reference Signal \(DMRS\) to each UE that enables the UE to determine the UE-specific beamforming weights to decode the PDSCH \(for reception in the downlink\), containing the multiplexed MIMO layer data transmissions. The configuration of DMRS plays an important role on the performance of the network, e.g., for a fast-fading channel, an additional DMRS symbol can be provided per slot trading off higher overhead; for higher traffic-load, configuration type 2 can be used trading off frequency domain density; for low-latency KPI requirements, mapping type B can be used, etc.
trace: 4.4 Massive MIMO optimization --> 4.4.2 Entities/resources involved in the use case --> 4.4.3.4 AI/ML based CSI-RS and DMRS configuration optimization

text_preview: Specifically,

text:
* the SMO/Non-RT RIC framework shall train AI/ML models to solve a joint two-stage optimization problem. In the first stage, the configurations of CSI-RS transmission and CSI-feedback reporting are optimized for each cell. In the second stage, the GoB-based UE-specific beams and the configuration of DMRS are optimized for each cell.
  * When the training is completed, the SMO/Non-RT RIC framework shall deploy the AI/ML model trained to optimize GoB-based UE-specific beams and DMRS configurations to the Near-RT RIC.
  * After that, based on the network dynamics, the SMO/Non-RT RIC framework shall update/modify the configurations of CSI-RS transmissions and CSI-feedback reporting at the E2 nodes \(e.g., O-DU\).
  * Based on the network dynamics and the trained AI/ML model received from the SMO/Non-RT RIC framework, the Near-RT RIC shall update/modify the UE-specific GoB-based beams and the DMRS configurations at the E2 nodes \(e.g., O-DU\) for a sequence of slots.

text: Based on the end-to-end requirements for the QoE optimization use case specified in \[32\] and in \[28\], some high-level functional description and requirements over Near-RT RIC and E2 interface are introduced.
trace: 4.5 QoE optimization
text_preview: Based on the end-to-end requirements for the QoE optimization use case specified in \[32\] and in \[28\], some high-level functional description and requirements over Near-RT RIC and E2 interface are introduced.

text: 4.5.1 Background and goal of the use case
trace: 4.5 QoE optimization --> 4.5.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: 4.5.1 Background and goal of the use case

text: The highly demanding 5G native applications like cloud VR are both bandwidth consuming and latency sensitive. However, for such traffic-intensive and highly interactive applications, current semi-static QoS framework can be insufficient to satisfy diversified QoE requirements especially taking into account potentially significant fluctuation of radio transmission capability. It is expected that QoE estimation/prediction can help deal with such uncertainty and improve the efficiency of radio resources, and eventually improve user experience. RAN Analytics Information \(RAI\) as RAN service can be exposed to RAI service consumers for specific UE \(as specified in O-RAN.WG1.O-RAN-Architecture-Description-v06.00 \[30\], clause 4.5\) or for groups of UE \(per slice, per cell, per PLMN, etc.\). RAI is envisioned to be helpful for the applications to improve the user experience.
trace: 4.5 QoE optimization --> 4.5.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: Highly demanding 5G apps like cloud VR consume bandwidth and are latency sensitive. Current QoS frameworks can't meet diversified QoE requirements due to fluctuating radio transmission capabilities. RAI (RAN Analytics Information) estimates/predicts QoE, improving resource efficiency and user experience.

text: Near-RT RIC and E2 interface are leveraged to support this use case. Measurement data through E2 interface, e.g., cell level data, UE level data, can be acquired and processed via ML algorithms to support traffic recognition, QoE prediction, and QoS enforcement decisions. When requested, the analytics information, e.g., traffic rate, latency, packet loss rate, is exposed to the RAI service consumers to help applications execute logical control.
trace: 4.5 QoE optimization --> 4.5.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: Near-RT RIC and E2 interface support this use case by acquiring cell and UE level data through ML algorithms for traffic recognition, QoE prediction, and QoS enforcement decisions. Analytics information is exposed to RAI service consumers upon request, helping applications execute logical control.

text: 4.5.2 Entities/resources involved in the use case
trace: 4.5 QoE optimization --> 4.5.2 Entities/resources involved in the use case
text_preview: 4.5.2 Entities/resources involved in the use case

text:
* 1\) Near-RT RIC:   
    * a\) Support receiving request or subscription messages from RAI service consumer.
    * b\) Support receiving network state and UE performance report from RAN.
    * c\) Support data analysis and executing the AI/ML models to infer RAN analytics information, e.g., QoE prediction, and available bandwidth prediction.
    * d\) Support exposure RAN analytics information to RAI service consumer.
  * 2\) RAN: 
    * a\) Support network state and UE performance report with required granularity to Near-RT RIC over E2 interface.
  * 3\) RAI service consumer: 
    * a\) Request or subscribe to RAN analytics information from the Near-RT RIC.
    * b\) Support UE identification using data structure as specified in O-RAN.WG1.O-RAN-Architecture-Description-v06.00 \[30\], clause 4.

text: 4.6 Network energy saving
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving
text_preview: 4.6 Network energy saving

text: This use case provides the motivation, description, and requirements for Near RT RIC and E2 interface to support network energy saving, whose end-to-end requirements are specified in \[32\].
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving
text_preview: This use case provides the motivation, description, and requirements for Near RT RIC and E2 interface to support network energy saving, whose end-to-end requirements are specified in \[32\].

text: The RAN is responsible for the majority of the Energy Consumption \(EC\) of a mobile network, and the O-RU consumes the largest part of the energy consumption of the RAN. The rarefication of fossil fuel-based energy resources and the urgent need to reduce CO2 emissions make energy saving a strategic goal for network operators, in addition to the significant energy related OPEX reduction requirement.
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving
text_preview: The RAN consumes most of a mobile network's energy (EC). The O-RU uses the largest share of RAN EC. With rarefied fossil fuels and urgent need to reduce CO2, energy saving is a strategic goal for operators, alongside significant OPEX reduction.

text: Energy consumption can be reduced by improving the Energy Efficiency \(EE\) of the network, and by introducing different Energy Saving \(ES\) mechanisms. Several ES mechanisms are related to switching off certain components and resources in the network and differ from one another by their time scale. In a longer time-scale of minutes, hours and above, and when the cell load is low, ES can be achieved by switching off one or more carriers or the cell itself. At the same or shorter time-scale, from seconds to minutes, ES can be achieved by switching off RF channels \(including possibly array of antennas\) of a Massive-MIMO \(mMIMO\) system. At a shorter time-scale corresponding to a symbol, subframe and frame, Advanced Sleep Modes \(ASM\) can be considered \(see ORAN-WG1.Use Cases Energy Saving Technical Report R003 v02.00 \[i.4\], 3GPP TR 28.813 \[i.5\] and 3GPP TS 28.310 \[33\]\).
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving
text_preview: Energy consumption can be reduced by improving Energy Efficiency and introducing different Energy Saving mechanisms. ES differs in time scale, ranging from minutes to seconds. Low cell load enables switching off carriers or cells at longer scales, while RF channels of Massive-MIMO systems are switched off using Advanced Sleep Modes (ASM).

text: The ES use cases are divided into three sub-use cases, which have different properties, the time scale of the control and the controlled system involved:
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving
text_preview: The ES use cases are divided into three sub-use cases, which have different properties, the time scale of the control and the controlled system involved:

text:
* 1\. Carrier and cell switch off/on  
  * 2\. RF channel reconfiguration
  * 3\. Advanced Sleep Modes
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving
text_preview:
* 1\. Carrier and cell switch off/on  
  * 2\. RF channel reconfiguration
  * 3\. Advanced Sleep Modes

text: Another mechanism to achieve ES is to apply PRB blanking optimization. Blanking the PRBs saves power in many components in the O-RU due to the reduced input/output power and processing load. PRB blanking also supports interference reduction in a multi-cell environment. PRB blanking optimization is applicable to all three time-scales \(longer time-scale of minutes or above, shorter time-scale from seconds to minutes as well as even shorter time-scale corresponding to a symbol, subframe and frame\).
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving
text_preview: Applying PRB blanking optimization reduces power in O-RU components by minimizing input/output power and processing load. This also supports interference reduction in multi-cell environments, applicable across three time-scales: minutes or above, seconds to minutes, and symbol-level.

text: 4.6.1 Carrier and cell switch off/on
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.1 Carrier and cell switch off/on
text_preview: 4.6.1 Carrier and cell switch off/on

text: 4.6.1.1 Background and goal of the use case
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.1 Carrier and cell switch off/on --> 4.6.1.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: 4.6.1.1 Background and goal of the use case

text: Carrier and cell switch off/on control by the Non-RT or Near-RT RIC can consider overall network energy efficiency instead of local optimization. In addition to the ES optimization in the SMO/Non-RT RIC, optimizing network EC in the Near-RT RIC brings significant gains due to more UE centric, near-real-time intelligent control capabilities with finer granularity. The AI/ML models' functionality in the Near-RT RIC can include prediction of future traffic, user mobility, resource usage, QoS and QoE on a per UE basis and may also predict expected energy efficiency enhancements, resource usage, and network performance for different carrier and cell switching off/on options. Based on the predicted results, optimized ES control actions or policies can be given by the Near-RT RIC to E2 nodes in near-real-time manner to track the dynamic network conditions. ES control also includes preparation actions \(before carrier and cells are switched off\) and post control actions \(after carrier and cells are switched on\) such as checking ongoing emergency calls and warning messages, enabling/disabling/modifying carrier aggregation and/or dual connectivity, steering traffic and handing over UEs from source cells/carriers to other cells/carriers, changing MU-MIMO layers, beam scheduling policies and SSB burst configurations etc, which can be handled in the Near-RT RIC by the intelligent and UE centric RAN control capabilities coordinated with the SMO/Non-RT RIC.
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.1 Carrier and cell switch off/on --> 4.6.1.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: The Non-RT or Near-RT RIC prioritizes network energy efficiency over local optimization, leveraging near-real-time UE-centric control capabilities. AI models predict future traffic and user behavior to optimize ES control actions, applying real-time optimized policies to E2 nodes via intelligent RAN control coordinated with SMO/Non-RT RIC.

text: The goal of Near-RT RIC energy saving is to interpret the policies received over A1 and to determine the optimum changes it can make according to these policies. More specifically, Near-RT RIC triggers E2 procedure and related control/policies so as to obtain network performance that would fulfill the criteria identified in the A1 policies. It may also leverage the A1 enrichment information to make more informed decisions. Traffic steering may reuse mechanisms provided by other use cases to affect the changes necessary to achieve its goals. The Near-RT RIC may also work in background processing without the A1 policy guidance from the Non-RT RIC.

text_preview: The goal of Near-RT RIC energy saving is to interpret A1 policies and determine optimal changes based on these policies. It triggers E2 procedure with A1 enrichment information to meet network performance criteria, potentially reusing traffic steering mechanisms from other use cases or working in background processing without A1 policy guidance.

text: There are three general ES processing modes and the transitions between them. The three processing modes, baseline, background and A1 policy-based, as described in clause 4.1.3 for traffic steering use case applies to the energy saving use case as is except that the modes represent the way the Near-RT RIC operates on a given E2 node rather than UE specific.

text: 3\) Carriers and cell switch off/on control: Depending on the traffic condition, certain number of carriers and cells can be switched off by the Near-RT RIC by sending guidance to the E2 node when the traffic is low in order to save energy. When the network conditions deteriorate \(e.g., congested traffic, frequent handover failure and/or RA failure\), carrier/cell switchon control command could be sent to E2 node in E2 policy/control to activate the cell/carrier from energy saving and hence ensure network performance.
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.1.4.1 Control over E2
text_preview: 3\) Carriers and cell switch off/on control: Near-RT RIC can switch off carriers and cells when traffic is low to save energy. When network conditions deteriorate (e.g., congested traffic, handover failures), it activates cells/carriers via E2 policy/control to ensure network performance.

text: NOTE: Once E2 node receives the guidance from Near-RT RIC for switching off/on a cell/carrier, it is not expected that the cell/carrier can be switched off immediately. The E2 node can take time to do all necessary actions to prepare for switching off/on the carrier/cell and there is also a delay in O-RU and open fronthaul interface for switching off/on the cell/carrier. However, it is still expected, as specified in \[32\], that the Near-RT RIC to send this intent to the E2 node to start the process for cell/carrier switching off/on after the network performance and energy efficiency are jointly optimized through for example traffic steering and QoS/QoE optimisation by the Near-RT RIC through 1\) and 2\). The E2 node \(e.g., O-CU-CP\) can optionally do traffic steering and OoS optimisation upon receiving this command from the Near-RT RIC before triggering the cell/carrier switching off/on.

text: During DL transmission or UL reception, certain O-RU components \(e.g., PA, LNA and baseband etc\) can be powered off during blank OFDM symbols and slots. For power saving at the symbol level, PA and LNA can be turned off since their transition period \(on to off and off to on\) can be in a few microseconds \(micro sleep\). For power saving at slot level, additional HW can be turned off to save more energy if the transition time allowed is in a few milliseconds \(light sleep\). For power saving at frame level, even more HW can be turned off \(e.g., only maintain O-RU M-plane processing\) however higher transition delay, in 100

text: The goal of Near-RT RIC energy saving is to interpret the policies received over A1 and to determine the optimum changes it can make according to these policies. More specifically, Near-RT RIC triggers E2 procedure and related control/policies so as to obtain network performance that would fulfill the criteria identified in the A1 policies. It may also leverage the A1 enrichment information to make more informed decisions. Traffic steering may reuse mechanisms provided by other use cases to affect the changes necessary to achieve its goals. The Near-RT RIC may also work in background processing without the A1 policy guidance from the Non-RT RIC.

@startuml
    autonumber
    skinparam ParticipantPadding 4
    skinparam BoxPadding 8
    skinparam defaultFontSize 12
    Box "Service Management and Orchestration" #gold
     Participant OAM as "OAM Functions"

    Box "O-RAN" #lightpink
     Participant near as "Near-RT RIC" 
     Participant ran as "E2 Node" 
    End box
    group OUTER LOOP CONTROL
     OAM <--> ran : (Mode 2) <<O1>> RAN Data collection
     OAM --> non: (Mode 2) ES related performance information
     non --> non: (Mode 2) Collected data evaluation and policy creation
     non --> near : (Mode 2) <<A1>> A1 policy setup or update
     non --> near: (opt.) <<A1-EI>> ES related A1 enrichment information
     near <--> ran: (Mode 1) <<E2>> RAN Data collection
     near --> near: (Mode 1) Collected data evaluation and policy creation
     group INNER LOOP CONTROL
     near -> ran : <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST(UE context & measurement metrics)
     ran -> near: <<E2>> RIC INDICATION (UE context & E2 measurement metrics)
     near -> near: Evaluation, potential improvement to energy efficiency
     near -> ran : (opt.) <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION REQUEST (ES optimisation POLICY)
     near -> ran : (opt.) <<E2>> RIC CONTROL REQUEST (ES optimisation RIC CONTROL)
     end
     non <-- near: (Mode 2) <<A1>> A1 policy feedback
    end
    non --> near: (Mode 2) <<A1>> A1 policy delete
    near -> near: ES optimization stopped
    near-> ran: <<E2>> RIC SUBSCRIPTION DELETE
    @enduml

text: 4.6.3.1 Background and goal of the use case
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.3 RF channel reconfiguration --> 4.6.3.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: 4.6.3.1 Background and goal of the use case

text: In mobile networks, massive-MIMO array antennas are used to implement beamforming techniques, which boost the cell coverage, capacity, and spectrum efficiency for enhanced mobile broadband services. Due to the massive number of the active antenna elements and RF channels used in the massive-MIMO array, it can consume significantly more energy than conventional antenna solution. The goal of the RF channel reconfiguration energy saving use case is to reduce the power consumption of O-RUs for massive-MIMO by dynamically reconfiguring the number of active Tx/Rx array antenna elements. When the traffic load is low, fewer beams or MU-MIMO spatial layers are needed, therefore, fewer Tx/Rx array antenna elements can be active which can be reconfigured from Near-RT RIC dynamically leading to significant power savings. The number of active antenna element and the antenna element layout also have an impact to the signal coverage and spatial channel orthogonality translating to impact to the UE service of quality, which need to be handled by the Near-RT RIC to avoid the impact to the performance or finding the trade-off between energy saving and performance.
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.3 RF channel reconfiguration --> 4.6.3.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: massive - mimo array antennas use beamforming for enhanced mobile broadband services , consuming more energy than conventional solutions . to reduce power consumption , tx / rx elements are dynamically reconfigured based on traffic load . low loads require fewer beams or mu - mimo spatial layers , leading to significant power savings . the near - rt ric balances

text: The goal of Near-RT RIC energy saving is to interpret the policies received over A1 interface. Based on policy and the current or predicted traffic and channel conditions, the Near-RT RIC then derive the best choices for O-RU Tx/Rx array configurations including e.g. number of active antenna element, antenna element layout, SU/MU MIMO layers etc and provide guided configurations to the O-DU. Following the guidance, O-DU may decide to disable \("putting to sleep"\) some or all array elements in a tx-array or rx-array \(or both\) accordingly via the O-FH C-plane in order to save energy \(see O-RAN.WG4.CUS.0-R003-v14 \[38\], clause 7.2.9.2.3\).
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.3 RF channel reconfiguration --> 4.6.3.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: The goal of Near-RT RIC energy saving is to interpret A1 interface policies, considering traffic and channel conditions. It derives optimal O-RU Tx/Rx array configurations, including antenna elements and MIMO layers. The O-DU disables some or all array elements via the O-FH C-plane to save energy.

text: 4.6.4.1 Background and goal of the use case
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.4 PRB blanking optimization --> 4.6.4.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: 4.6.4.1 Background and goal of the use case

text: Blanking the PRBs saves power in many components in the O-RU due to the reduced input/output power and processing load. In addition, PRB blanking is being supported in clause 8.4.2 of WG4 Control, User and Synchronization Plane Specification as Data blanking \[38\] to meet objectives such as energy saving. Specifically, in clause 8.4.2.2, it said "PRB blanking is an inherent feature of the frequency-domain-based fronthaul split 7-2x, where unallocated PRBs are not sent across the fronthaul interface to reduce the fronthaul throughput. An unallocated PRB is a PRB with all REs unallocated". Currently, an O-DU can blank the PRBs during scheduling taking local performance targets such as energy consumption into consideration, and then signal the blanked or activated PRBs to O-RU via C-plane Section Type 1 messages. However, the Near-RT RIC is not able to send configurations/policies regarding PRBs to be blanked to an O-DU to influence the MAC scheduler behaviours for optimizing PRB allocations to meet different performance targets in a network with multiple cells. PRB blanking has also been leveraged to achieve interference optimization in a network with multiple cells as specified in use case 26 of WG1 Use Cases Detailed
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.4 PRB blanking optimization --> 4.6.4.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: Blanking PRBs saves power in O-RU components by reducing input/output power and processing load. Clause 8.4.2 of WG4 Control, User and Synchronization Plane Specification supports data blanking for energy saving [38]. An O-DU can schedule PRB blanking based on local performance targets like energy consumption.

text: Specification R004 v15.00.01 \[49\]. PRB blanking optimization by the Near-RT RIC can consider overall network performance improvements for both uplink and downlink including energy efficiency with system-level optimization instead of local-level optimization by an O-DU alone. Furthermore, the AI/ML models' functionality in the Near-RT RIC can include prediction of future traffic, user mobility, resource usage, QoS and QoE on a per UE basis and may also predict expected energy efficiency enhancements, resource usage, network performance and interference reduction for different PRB blanking optimization options. Based on the predicted results, optimized PRBs blanking control actions or policies can be given by the Near-RT RIC to E2 nodes in near-real-time manner.
trace: 4.6 Network energy saving --> 4.6.4 PRB blanking optimization --> 4.6.4.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: Specification R004 v15.00.01 \[49\]. Near-RT RIC optimizes network performance through system-level optimization, predicting future traffic and energy efficiency using AI/ML models. The RIC provides optimized control actions to E2 nodes in near-real-time based on predicted results.

text: The Near-RT RIC sends the two-dimensional \(in both frequency and time domains\) PRB blanking configurations or policies for uplink and/or downlink to each O-DU to consider for cells of interest in a multi-cell environment based on the evaluation of performance measurements collected and performance targets required. The performance measurements collected include e.g., EC, EE achieved, QoS including throughput and latency as well as interference. The performance targets include e.g., EC, EE, QoS and interference reduction. The Near-RT RIC decides the two-dimensional PRB blanking configurations or policies which include how many PRBs to blank and where those PRBs are in the frequency and time domain based on the trade-off analysis. The O-DU takes the PRB blanking configurations or policies as an input for its scheduler to make final resource allocations decision.

text_preview: The Near-RT RIC sends 2D PRB blanking configs/policies (uplink/downlink) to each O-DU, considering performance measurements and targets. The 2D configs include how many PRBs to blank and where they are in frequency/time domain based on trade-off analysis.

text: interference management techniques to mitigate inter-cell interference to improve QoS for users, especially at the cell edge. How to detect and then optimize interference is of great importance for cellular wireless networks.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: interference management techniques to mitigate inter-cell interference to improve QoS for users, especially at the cell edge. How to detect and then optimize interference is of great importance for cellular wireless networks.

text: 3GPP specifies multiple categories of interference management techniques to support interference optimization. The first category is based on the principle of inter-cell interference coordination. It has three sub-categories: Inter-Cell Interference Coordination \(ICIC\), enhanced ICIC \(eICIC\), and further enhanced ICIC \(feICIC\) where ICIC works in the frequency domain, eICIC in the time domain and feICIC in the UE domain.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: 3GPP specifies multiple interference management techniques to support optimization. The first category is based on inter-cell interference coordination (ICIC), with three sub-categories: ICIC (frequency domain), enhanced ICIC (time domain), and further enhanced ICIC (UE domain).

text: For ICIC, if the two-dimensional \(in frequency and time\) RBs for data channels to be scheduled in a cell can be shared and coordinated with other neighboring cells, interference of UEs near the cell edge can be mitigated. ICIC can leverage the following mechanisms.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: For ICIC, if the two-dimensional \(in frequency and time\) RBs for data channels to be scheduled in a cell can be shared and coordinated with other neighboring cells, interference of UEs near the cell edge can be mitigated. ICIC can leverage the following mechanisms.

text:
* Restricting scheduling RBs: The RBs used by a group of users in one geographical area \(e.g., in the cell edge\) for a cell is not scheduled by the neighboring cells. It is to avoid simultaneous transmission in the cell edge from neighboring cells.  
  * Adjustment of the power level on physical channels.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview:
* Restricting scheduling RBs: The RBs used by a group of users in one geographical area \(e.g., in the cell edge\) for a cell is not scheduled by the neighboring cells. It is to avoid simultaneous transmission in the cell edge from neighboring cells.  
  * Adjustment of the power level on physical channels.

text: ICIC can be implemented in a static or dynamic way. Static ICIC is achieved when the network operator manually manages cell configurations which become overly complex in practical deployments and are typically slow to adapt to changes in the network. Dynamic ICIC is required for fast adaptation of the interference scenarios, and exchange of signaling messages over X2/Xn interfaces among neighboring cells to convey scheduling decisions are needed to support interference optimization \[12\]\[19\]. The ICIC concept was the origin of PRB blanking.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: ICIC can be implemented statically or dynamically. Static ICIC is impractical due to complex cell configurations, while dynamic ICIC enables fast adaptation to network changes and interference scenarios. This approach requires exchanging signaling messages over X2/Xn interfaces for scheduling decisions, supporting interference optimization.

text: For UL, the High Interference Indicator \(HII\) and Overload Indicator \(OI\) are available \[12\]. The HII informs the neighboring cells of the RBs to be scheduled for UEs as a proactive mechanism. With this information, the neighboring cells can avoid scheduling the same RBs for the UEs near the interfering cell. The OI informs the neighboring cells of the interference levels received on various two-dimensional resources \(low, medium and high\) as a reactive mechanism. With this information, the neighboring cells can a\) reduce transmit power level, b\) not schedule those RBs for UEs near the cell edge or c\) not schedule those RBs at all.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview:
For UL, High Interference Indicator (HII) and Overload Indicator (OI) are available [12]. HII informs neighboring cells of scheduled RBs to avoid interference. OI informs them of received interference levels on low, medium, and high resources, allowing:

a) Reduced transmit power
b) Scheduling near cell edge
c) No scheduling

text: For DL, the Relative Narrowband Transmit Power \(RNTP\) informs the neighboring cells of the transmit power level per RB, including the RNTP threshold and RNTP bitmap of all RBs \[12\]. In the RNTP bitmap each bit indicates if the transmit power of an RB would exceed the RNTP threshold. With this information, the power allocation for UEs near the cell edge can be dynamically adjusted in a coordinated way.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: For DL, the Relative Narrowband Transmit Power (RNTP) informs neighboring cells of transmit power per RB, including the RNTP threshold and bitmap. The bitmap indicates if an RB's transmit power would exceed the threshold, enabling dynamic power allocation for UEs near the cell edge in a coordinated manner.

text: A cell can request load measurements from neighboring cells via Resource Status Reporting where the load measurements include DL and UL PRB usages \[19\].
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: A cell can request load measurements from neighboring cells via Resource Status Reporting where the load measurements include DL and UL PRB usages \[19\].

text: For eICIC, cells exchange coordinated messages with its neighbors to allow the scheduler to create Almost Blank Subframes \(ABS\) in the time domain to mitigate interference at the UEs. The ABS contains no data traffic, but common Reference Signals \(RSs\) are still transmitted. Muted subframes should be avoided in subframes that transmit critical information Critical control channels \(including System Information Block \[SIB\] 1 and paging\), and broadcast \(Master Information Block \[MIB\]\) information are required in these subframes to avoid radio link failure for legacy UEs.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: For eICIC, cells exchange coordinated messages with neighbors to create Almost Blank Subframes (ABS). ABS contains no data traffic but transmits common Reference Signals (RSs). Muted subframes should be avoided in critical information subframes, as they require System Information Block 1 and paging, and Master Information Block (MIB) information.

text: For feICIC \(also called the terminal-based interference management technique\), interference cancellation is implemented at the UE for the critical control physical channels or signals that eICIC cannot handle \(e.g., synchronization signals, reference signals, broadcast channel, etc.\).
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: For feICIC \(also called the terminal-based interference management technique\), interference cancellation is implemented at the UE for the critical control physical channels or signals that eICIC cannot handle \(e.g., synchronization signals, reference signals, broadcast channel, etc.\).

text: The second category of interference management is based on carrier aggregation. In carrier aggregation, multiple carriers are aggregated at a cell. There are three types of carrier aggregation.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: The second category of interference management is based on carrier aggregation. In carrier aggregation, multiple carriers are aggregated at a cell. There are three types of carrier aggregation.

text:
* Contiguous aggregation of component carriers in a single band
  * Non-contiguous aggregation of component carriers in a single band
  * Non-contiguous aggregation of component carriers over multiple bands
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview:
* Contiguous aggregation of component carriers in a single band
  * Non-contiguous aggregation of component carriers in a single band
  * Non-contiguous aggregation of component carriers over multiple bands

text: The third category is based on Coordinated Multipoint \(CoMP\), which works in the spatial domain. CoMP is for multiple cells to coordinate with each other to jointly transmit and receive information to a single UE. CoMP performs coordinated scheduling and beam forming on a UE to improve performance in an interference environment \(by minimizing interference\). CoMP is similar to the soft handover concept in Code Division Multiple Access \(CDMA\).
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: The third category is based on Coordinated Multipoint (CoMP), which works in the spatial domain. CoMP enables multiple cells to coordinate with each other to jointly transmit and receive information to a single UE. It improves performance by minimizing interference through coordinated scheduling and beam forming.

text: To trigger interference optimization, interference detection \(including detecting the interference energy, classifying the interference source types, identifying the interference levels, and locating the interference source in terms of a geographical location\) is required. In addition to LTE and 5G interference, other non-3GPP types of interference experienced in a 5G network, including internal and external RF interference, also need to be detected and optimized.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization
text_preview: To trigger interference optimization, detecting interference energy, source types, levels, and location is required. This includes LTE and 5G interference, as well as internal and external RF interference in non-3GPP networks.

text: Thanks to the open interface, the virtualization and intelligent functionalities provided by the O-RAN architecture, multi-cellbased collaborative real-time interference detection and optimization schemes can be realized. The operation and performance evaluation for interference detection and optimization in real-time should be conducted based on interference-related data focusing on a specific UE, UE group, RAN slice, PRBs or mMIMO beams, which is the primary target of improvement. The Near-RT RIC ensures optimal radio resource allocation for a UE, UE group, RAN slice, PRBs, and mMIMO beams through the E2 interface to improve the efficiency of radio resource utilization and interference optimization.
trace: 4.7 Interference detection and optimization

Real-time evaluation focuses on specific targets like UE, RAN slice, or PRBs. The Near-RT RIC optimizes radio resource allocation through E2 interface to improve efficiency and interference optimization.

The following is a list of interference optimization mechanisms that manage resources in time, frequency, space and power domains to achieve the objective of interference optimization.

text:
* Traditional cellular RF design techniques: antenna down-tilt and antenna azimuth orientation
  * Traditional cellular RF design technique: transmit power level adjustment at E2 node
  * Power control
  * PRB blanking
  * Carrier aggregation
  * CoMP
  * Beam control \(including beam muting as beam forming such as beam nulling\)

text_preview:
Traditional cellular RF design techniques include:

* Antenna down-tilt and azimuth orientation
* Transmit power level adjustment at E2 node
* Power control
* PRB blanking
* Carrier aggregation
* Coordinated Multi-Point (CoMP)
* Beam control, including beam muting and nulling.

text: Carrier aggregation reduces interference by selecting the carriers with less interference to aggregate.

text: CoMP reduces interference by selecting cells that experience less interference.

text_preview: CoMP reduces interference by selecting cells that experience less interference.

text: Beam muting reduces interference in the spatial domain by muting one or more SSB beams and / or traffic beams in the MIMO Grid of Beams \(GoB\) mode.

text_preview: Beam muting reduces interference in the spatial domain by muting one or more SSB beams and / or traffic beams in the MIMO Grid of Beams \(GoB\) mode.

text: Beam forming reduces interference in the spatial domain by forming nulls to cancel interference in MIMO GoB and non-GoB modes.
