text: By analyzing the interference detection results, with the support of AI/ML, the Near-RT RIC sends control and / or policies regarding interference optimization mechanisms to an O-DU to influence the MAC scheduler behaviors for interference optimization in a network with multiple cells. The Near-RT RIC can achieve overall network performance improvements including interference optimization for both uplink and downlink with system-level optimization instead of local-level optimization by an O-DU alone. Furthermore, the AI/ML models' functionality in the Near-RT RIC can include prediction of future traffic, user mobility, resource usage, and QoS/QoE on a per UE basis as well as prediction of network performance and effectiveness of interference reduction for different interference optimization mechanisms. Based on the predicted results, interference optimization control and / or policy can be given by the Near-RT RIC to E2 nodes in a near-real-time manner.
trace: 4.7.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: The Near-RT RIC optimizes MAC scheduler behaviors for interference reduction in a network with multiple cells. Using AI/ML, it predicts future traffic, user mobility, and resource usage, then provides near-real-time interference optimization control/policies to E2 nodes based on predicted results.

text: The interference optimization objective includes performance targets in QoS and interference reduction on a specific UE, UE group, RAN slice, PRBs or mMIMO beams such that the impact of interference on the QoS metric of a specific UE, UE group, RAN slice or cell can be reduced by a certain percentage. One example of the performance targets in QoS is the average DL throughput and UL throughput of the UEs near the cell edge to achieve. One example of performance targets in interference reduction is a 90% interference reduction target for a group of UEs in a cell which means that the average channel quality \(e.g., CQI\) for the specified group of UEs under interference can be improved by applying interference optimization mechanisms to a 90% level compared to those when there is no interference.
trace: 4.7.1 Background and goal of the use case
text_preview: The interference optimization objective aims to reduce interference impact on QoS metrics, such as average DL and UL throughput near cell edges or channel quality for specific UEs/UE groups/RAN slices/cells by a certain percentage (e.g., 90% reduction). This is achieved through performance targets in QoS and interference reduction.

text: The Downlink and Uplink Throughput Per Network Slice are NG.116 attributes used in the definition and deployment of a network slice. They become maxDlThptPerSlice and maxUlThptPerSlice parameters in A1 polic\(ies\). The maximum downlink throughput per slice defines the aggregated data rate in the downlink for all UEs together in the network slice. This parameter is defined in GSMA GST NEST NG.116 Downlink throughput per network slice \[22\], clause 3.4.5. See also 3GPP TS 28.541 \[5\], clause 6.3.4 which defines the SliceProfile that captures some of the parameters from GSMA depending on the slice type. The parameter places an upper limit on the capacity of the slice so that the slice does not over-utilize available network resources and thereby provides a target to guide resource utilization.
trace: A.1 Example use cases for RAN slice SLA assurance --> A.1.1 Downlink and uplink throughput per slice
text_preview: NG.116 defines maxDlThptPerSlice (downlink) and maxUlThptPerSlice (uplink) per network slice, setting an aggregated data rate limit to prevent over-utilization of available resources. This parameter guides resource utilization and informs network planning.

text: The following explanation describes the relevance to the Near-RT RIC. These attributes are sent by the Non-RT RIC to the Near-RT RIC\(s\) together with the scope identifier \(S-NSSAI\) and optional cell list or tracking area list. The Near-RT RICs split the A1 policy guidance from the Non-RT RIC. Thus, the subtending Near-RT RICs each provide guidance to the cells of their E2 nodes \(O-DU, O-CU-UP, O-CU-CP\) involved in the slice.
trace: A.1 Example use cases for RAN slice SLA assurance --> A.1.1 Downlink and uplink throughput per slice
text_preview: Near-RT RICs receive attributes from Non-RT RICs with scope identifier S-NSSAI and optional cell/list information. Near-RT RICs split A1 policy guidance, providing it to cells of their E2 nodes (O-DU, O-CU-UP, O-CU-CP) involved in the slice.

text: For example, suppose there is an SLA parameter, Downlink throughput per network slice, with a value of 600,000 kilobits per second \(kbps\). The Non-RT RIC in this case has three subtending Near-RT RICs. Then, the Non-RT RIC might split the SLA parameter of 600,000 kbps into three A1 policies: maxDlThptPerSlice = 120,000 kbps for Near-RT RIC \#1; maxDlThptPerSlice = 180,000 kbps for Near-RT RIC \#2, and maxDlThptPerSlice = 300,000 kbps for Near-RT RIC \#3 for the respective slice. This example use case is shown in figure A.1.1-1.

The xApp\(s\) can utilize E2 interface to adjust throughput-related RAN parameters, such as adjusting PRB allocation levels The Near-RT RIC has influence over the operation of cells in a geographical area. text: 3GPP Release 17 will introduce the concept of a Network Slice Admission Control Function \(NSACF\), see reference \[\(TR23.700-40 S2-1908583\)\] and reference \[\(TS23.501 v17.1.1 clause 5.15.11\)\]. The purpose of the NSACF is to enforce some of the slice SLA parameters from a 5G core perspective. The NSACF handles slice-specific user admission control into the network based on NG.116 criterion. However, the NSACF has no knowledge of RAN and RAN resources; thus, it cannot control RAN resources. Therefore, there is no interaction between NSACF and the handling of these parameters by the Near-RT RIC. Thus, the usage of the SLA-related parameters by the Near-RT RIC xApp\(s\) are in the scope of gNBs and will complement the 5GC SLA enforcement but from the perspective of the RAN.

text_preview: 3GPP Release 17 introduces NSACF, enforcing slice SLA parameters from a 5G core perspective. However, it lacks knowledge of RAN resources, so there's no interaction with Near-RT RIC for RAN resource management. GNBs handle SLA-related parameters, complementing 5GC SLA enforcement from the RAN side.

text: A.1.2 Guaranteed downlink and uplink throughput per slice
trace: A.1 Example use cases for RAN slice SLA assurance --> A.1.1 Downlink and uplink throughput per slice --> A.1.2 Guaranteed downlink and uplink throughput per slice
text_preview: A.1.2 Guaranteed downlink and uplink throughput per slice

text: The Guaranteed Downlink Throughput Quota and Guaranteed Uplink Throughput Quota are attributes used in the definition and deployment of a network slice in NG.116. They are used in A1 policies as guaDlThptPerSlice and guaUlThptPerSlice. The guaranteed downlink/uplink throughput quota describes the guaranteed throughput or data rate supported by the network slice for the aggregate of all GBR QoS flows in downlink/uplink belonging to the set of all UEs using the network slice. This parameter is defined in GSMA GST NEST NG.116 Downlink/Uplink throughput per network slice \[22\], clause 3.4.5. See also 3GPP TS 28.541 \[5\], clause 6.3.4 which defines the SliceProfile which captures some of the parameters from GSMA depending on the slice type. The Maximum Ul/Dl Throughput per Network Slice parameters \(clause 3.3.3.1.1\) place an upper limit on the capacity of the slice while the Guaranteed Ul/Dl Throughput Quota parameters ensure a certain level of throughput. Thus, these two parameters complement each other: one giving a lower bound and the other giving an upper bound. For the upper bound \(maximum Ul/Dl throughput per network slice\) this ensures that the slice does not overutilize available network resources while for the lower bound \(guaranteed Dl/Ul throughput quota\) meets a minimum throughput for the slice.
trace: A.1 Example use cases for RAN slice SLA assurance --> A.1.1 Downlink and uplink throughput per slice --> A.1.2 Guaranteed downlink and uplink throughput per slice
text_preview: In NG.116, Guaranteed Downlink Throughput Quota (GDLT) and Guaranteed Uplink Throughput Quota (GUPT) define guaranteed throughput for GBR QoS flows using a slice. They balance capacity limits with minimum throughput requirements, ensuring resource utilization and meeting minimums.

The Near-RT RICs split the A1 policy guidance from the Non-RT RIC. Thus, the subtending Near-RT RICs each provide guidance to the cells of the E2 nodes \(O-DU, O-CU-UP, O-CU-CP\) involved in the slice.

text: For example, suppose there is an SLA parameter, Guaranteed Uplink Throughput Quota, with a value of 1,000,000 kilobits per second \(kbps\). The Non-RT RIC in this case has three sub-tending Near-RT RICs. Then, the Non-RT RIC might split the SLA parameter of 1,000,000 kbps into three A1 policies: guaUlThptPerSlice = 170,000 kbps for Near-RT RIC \#1; guaUlThptPerSlice = 230,000 kbps for Near-RT RIC \#2, and guaUlThptPerSlice = 600,000 kbps for Near-RT RIC \#3 for the respective slice.

text: The consumer of the guaUlThptPerSlice and guaDlThptPerSlice parameters is the Near-RT RIC via A1 policy. Slice SLA assurance-related xApp\(s\), within the Near-RT RIC, can apply or utilize this parameter to provide control of and throughput within the E2 nodes \(O-CU-UP, O-CU-CP, O-DU\). The xApp\(s\) can utilize E2 interface to adjust throughput-related RAN parameters, such as adjusting PRB allocation levels. The Near-RT RIC has influence over the operation of cells in a geographical area. The adjustment of the PRB allocation levels in MAC schedulers directly impacts the throughput achieved by the slice. Therefore, this parameter at the RAN level influences the throughput. There might be other throughput-related parameters that could be employed, such as MCS, which is left for future study.
